questions.question: What is the equilibrium expression ($K_{eq}$) for the reaction $\mathrm{N_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g)}$?
questions.answer: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[NO]^2}{[N_2][O_2]}$.

questions.question: Which aqueous solution turns universal indicator blue-purple?
questions.answer: Blue-purple indicates a strongly basic solution; only NaOH is a strong base.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name for $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2C({=}O){-}O{-}CH_3}$?
questions.answer: The acid part has five carbons (pentanoate) and the alkyl group on the single-bonded O is methyl.

questions.question: The Indigenous peoples of the Tiwi Islands in Northern Australia process yams (sweet potatoes) to make a food called Bitter Yam. Which of the following is an example of the use of solution equilibria to remove toxins from these yams?
questions.answer: Leaching soaks the yam in water so soluble toxins dissolve into the water, which is repeatedly replaced.

questions.question: A sample of 1-bromoethane is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What would be the most likely products of this reaction?
questions.answer: Substitution: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH + NaBr}$.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds are positional isomers?
questions.answer: They have the same carbon chain and functional group, differing only in the position of the C=O.

questions.question:
An unknown solution was tested with these results.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|}\hline \text{Test} & \text{Reaction}\\\hline \text{Flame test} & \text{Apple green}\\ \text{Dilute HCl added} & \text{No reaction}\\ \mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\text{ added} & \text{White precipitate}\\ \mathrm{AgNO_3}\text{ added} & \text{White precipitate}\\\hline\end{array}$$

What compound was in the solution?
questions.answer: Apple green flame and a sulfate precipitate indicate $Ba^{2+}$; no gas with HCl rules out carbonate; the $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ precipitate indicates $Cl^-$.

questions.question: Which equation demonstrates a limitation of the Brønsted–Lowry model of acids and bases?
questions.answer: This acid–base reaction involves no proton transfer, so Brønsted–Lowry theory cannot describe it.

questions.question: Which row ranks the compounds from lowest to highest pH?
questions.answer: Electron-withdrawing Cl atoms make trichloroethanoic acid the strongest acid; ethanamide is essentially neutral and ethanamine is basic.
options: trichloroethanoic acid, ethanoic acid, ethanamide, ethanamine
ethanoic acid, trichloroethanoic acid, ethanamine, ethanamide
ethanamine, ethanamide, trichloroethanoic acid, ethanoic acid
ethanamide, ethanamine, ethanoic acid, trichloroethanoic acid

questions.question:
Soaps and detergents have similar characteristics. Which set of criteria correctly identifies a detergent, but NOT a soap?

I. Ineffective in hard water

II. Only some are biodegradable

III. Always an ion

IV. Produced from natural fats or oils
questions.answer: Soaps (not detergents) fail in hard water, are always ionic and come from fats and oils. Only some detergents are biodegradable.

questions.question: At the end of an experiment a chemist had these materials to dispose of safely: (i) 120 mL of cyclohexane; (ii) 150 mL of unused 1 M $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$; (iii) a solid lead compound (from gravimetric analysis), dried and weighed on filter paper. Which gives an appropriate disposal method for (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively?
questions.answer: Organic solvents go to organic waste, dilute sodium sulfate is harmless, lead is a toxic heavy metal. Unused chemicals are never returned to stock bottles.
options: “Organic Liquids Only” waste; a stock bottle of Na₂SO₄ prepared for the experiment; rubbish bin
“Organic Liquids Only” waste; down the sink; “Heavy Metals Only” waste
“Aqueous Waste Only” container; “Aqueous Waste Only” container; rubbish bin
“Aqueous Waste Only” container; a stock bottle of Na₂SO₄ prepared for the experiment; “Heavy Metals Only” waste

questions.question: A monoprotic acid, HA, was titrated with $0.100\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ NaOH, giving the curve shown. What was the strength of the acid?
questions.answer: The equivalence point is above 7 (about 9) because the conjugate base of a weak acid hydrolyses to give a basic solution.
options: Strong acid since the initial pH is low
Strong acid since the equivalence point is 9
Weak acid since the final pH is high
Weak acid since the equivalence point is 9

questions.question: A monoprotic acid, HA, was titrated with $0.100\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ NaOH, giving the curve shown. Which indicator would be appropriate to use?
questions.answer: Phenolphthalein changes colour at pH about 8.3–10, matching the equivalence point of about 9.

questions.question:
$\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ dissociates sequentially:

$\mathrm{H_3PO_4(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + H_2PO_4^-(aq)}$

$\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + HPO_4^{2-}(aq)}$

$\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + PO_4^{3-}(aq)}$

Which of these species are amphiprotic?
questions.answer: Both can donate a proton and accept a proton.

questions.question: Coal is mostly carbon and is a limited resource. A student found: $\mathrm{C(s) + CO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2CO(g)}$, with $\Delta G<0$ (forward direction) when $T>1100$ K. How could this equation be used to produce more coal in the school laboratory?
questions.answer: Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (1 vs 2), shifting left and producing C(s). The other changes shift it right or have no useful effect.
options: Use a smaller container to decrease the volume of the vessel
Use some dry ice to add more carbon dioxide to the vessel
Use a larger container to decrease the pressure of the vessel
Use a hot water bath to increase the temperature in the vessel

questions.question: For $\mathrm{C(s) + CO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2CO(g)}$, a mixture of 200 g of coal (carbon) and 0.70 mol of CO was introduced into a 3.0 L vessel. At equilibrium 0.30 mol of $CO_2$ was present. What was the value of $K$ at this temperature?
An ester was produced in the school laboratory. Which set of equipment would have been used to produce it?
questions.answer: Esterification is carried out by heating under reflux, which returns volatile reactants to the flask.

questions.question: Analysis of an ester gave a percentage composition by mass of C 62.0% and H 10.4% (the remainder oxygen), and a molar mass of about $116\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. What is its molecular formula?
questions.answer: Mole ratio C : H : O $=\frac{62.0}{12.01}:\frac{10.4}{1.008}:\frac{27.6}{16.00}=3:6:1$. $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$ has $M=58$, so the formula is $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}$.

questions.question: 4-Hydroxybutanoic acid, $\mathrm{HO(CH_2)_3COOH}$, forms a polymer containing 1000 monomer units. Which is closest to the molar mass (g mol⁻¹) of this polymer?
questions.answer: $M=1000(104.1)-999(18.02)=8.6\times10^4$ g mol⁻¹ (condensation removes one water per link).

questions.question: An antacid containing magnesium oxide was tested. 40.6 g of antacid was dissolved in 500.0 mL of water, then diluted to 1.00 L. A 100 mL aliquot was reacted with 100 mL of $2.00\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ HCl. The excess acid required 19.7 mL of $0.200\text{ mol L}^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. What is the percentage of magnesium oxide in the antacid?
questions.answer: HCl used $=0.200-0.00394=0.19606$ mol, so $n(MgO)=0.09803$ mol per aliquot and 0.9803 mol in 1.00 L. Mass $=0.9803\times40.31=39.52$ g, which is $97.3\%$.

questions.question: How does the structure of soap help it to remove fats? You may use a diagram in your answer.
questions.answer:
A soap is the salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. $\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_{16}COO^-\,Na^+}$. It has two distinct parts:

- a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail (hydrophobic), which forms dispersion forces with non-polar fats;
- a charged carboxylate head (hydrophilic), which forms ion–dipole forces with water.

The tails embed in a fat droplet while the heads stay in the water. With agitation the fat lifts off the surface as a micelle: tails inside in the grease, negative heads on the outside. The like charges make micelles repel each other, so the fat stays suspended as an emulsion and is rinsed away.

questions.question: The diagram shows an unsaturated and a saturated fat chain segment, with the carbons of the unsaturated fat numbered. What shapes would the first and second carbons in the unsaturated fat display?
questions.answer: Carbon 1 (four single bonds): tetrahedral. Carbon 2 (part of the C=C double bond): trigonal planar.

questions.question: Unsaturated fats are liquids at room temperature but can be hardened into solids by converting them to saturated fats. Other than their state, how could a fat be tested to ensure it was unsaturated?
questions.answer:
Add bromine water and shake. An unsaturated fat undergoes an addition reaction across the C=C bond, so the orange-brown colour disappears (decolourises). A saturated fat leaves the colour unchanged in the absence of UV light.

$\mathrm{{>}C{=}C{<}\; + Br_2 \rightarrow {>}CBr{-}CBr{<}}$

questions.question: What type of reaction would be used to convert an unsaturated fat to a saturated fat?
questions.answer: An addition reaction: hydrogenation ($H_2$ with a Ni catalyst and heat).

questions.question: Crude oil contains many unsaturated hydrocarbons and can be used to produce polymers. Outline the structure and ONE property, with its related use, for an addition polymer.
questions.answer:
Polyethylene is made by addition polymerisation of ethene: $n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2 \rightarrow {-}(CH_2{-}CH_2)_{n}{-}}$

Structure: very long hydrocarbon chains of repeating $\mathrm{CH_2CH_2}$ units. In low-density polyethylene (LDPE) the chains are branched, so they pack loosely.

Property and use: the loose packing gives weaker dispersion forces between chains, making LDPE flexible, so it is used for cling wrap and plastic bags.

questions.question: Pink Lake is a salt lake in Victoria that dries during the summer months leaving a bed of pink salt (mainly sodium chloride). Explain how pink salt dissolves in rainwater. Use diagrams to support your answer.
questions.answer:
Solid NaCl is an ionic lattice of alternating $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ held by strong electrostatic attraction. Water molecules are polar (δ− on O, δ+ on H) and are held to each other by hydrogen bonds.

When rain falls on the salt, water molecules surround ions at the surface of the lattice and form ion–dipole attractions: the O atoms point towards $Na^+$, and the H atoms point towards $Cl^-$. The energy released by these many attractions is comparable to that needed to separate the ions and disrupt some water–water hydrogen bonds. Ions are pulled from the lattice and become hydrated, spreading through the solution:

$$\mathrm{NaCl(s) \rightarrow Na^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)}$$

Diagram description: left, a cubic lattice of alternating + and − ions; right, a $Na^+$ ion surrounded by water molecules with O inward, and a $Cl^-$ ion surrounded by water molecules with one H inward.

questions.question: Pink Lake is a salt lake whose salt is commercially harvested and may have been used by Aboriginal Australians in their diet. Analysis shows that as well as sodium chloride it contains traces of calcium, phosphate and copper. Why should the Pink Lake environment be monitored by chemists?
questions.answer:
Monitoring ensures the water and salt stay safe for organisms in the lake and for people who consume the salt.

- Copper is toxic to aquatic organisms and can bioaccumulate up the food chain, harming people; its level must stay within safe limits.
- Excess phosphate can cause algal blooms and eutrophication, depleting dissolved oxygen and killing aquatic life.
- High calcium makes water hard (scale, poor lathering of soap) and affects water suitability, though it is a smaller health concern.

Regular analysis detects changes (e.g. from runoff or industry) early enough to act.

questions.question: How have Aboriginal Australians used acid/base analysis techniques?
questions.answer:
Two examples:

1. Taste has been used to judge acidity of bush foods: e.g. Kakadu plum, rich in ascorbic acid, tastes very sour when unripe and less sour as it ripens.
2. Alkaline plant ash or lime has been mixed with leaves of plants such as pituri, raising the pH so that the active alkaloid is released in its free-base form and absorbed more readily.

questions.question: A student mixed 10 mL of 0.01 M $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ with 10 mL of 0.0001 M NaCl. Using calculations, demonstrate whether a precipitate would be produced.
questions.answer:
The possible precipitate is AgCl: $\mathrm{AgCl(s) \rightleftharpoons Ag^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)}$, $K_{sp}=1.77\times10^{-10}$.

After mixing the volume is 20 mL, so each concentration halves:

$[Ag^+]=5\times10^{-3}$ M, $[Cl^-]=5\times10^{-5}$ M

$Q=[Ag^+][Cl^-]=2.5\times10^{-7}$

Since $Q>K_{sp}$, a precipitate of AgCl forms.

questions.question: 10 mL of 0.01 M $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ is mixed with 10 mL of 0.0001 M NaCl, forming a precipitate of AgCl. What mass of precipitate is produced?
questions.answer:
$n(Ag^+)=1\times10^{-4}$ mol and $n(Cl^-)=1\times10^{-6}$ mol, so $Cl^-$ is limiting and $n(AgCl)=1\times10^{-6}$ mol (the amount left in solution is negligible).

$m=1\times10^{-6}\times143.35=1.4\times10^{-4}$ g

questions.question:
A student investigated how acid affects limestone (mostly calcium carbonate, with small amounts of calcium sulfate). Pieces of limestone were placed in 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid in three beakers and 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid in three others, as shown. Each day the limestone was removed, washed, dried, weighed and replaced.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Time (days)} & \text{Average mass in nitric acid (g)}\\\hline 0&48.08\\1&47.97\\2&47.94\\3&47.91\\4&47.91\\5&47.91\\\hline\end{array}$$

Draw a graph of the results for the nitric acid experiment.
questions.answer: Plot time (independent) on the x-axis and mass on the y-axis with a broken, evenly spaced scale from about 47.90 g, label both axes with units, plot all six points and draw a smooth curve of best fit that levels off at 47.91 g from day 3.

questions.question:
A student investigated how acid affects limestone (mostly calcium carbonate, with small amounts of calcium sulfate). Pieces of limestone were placed in 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid in three beakers and 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid in three others, as shown. Each day the limestone was removed, washed, dried, weighed and replaced.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Time (days)} & \text{Average mass in nitric acid (g)}\\\hline 0&48.08\\1&47.97\\2&47.94\\3&47.91\\4&47.91\\5&47.91\\\hline\end{array}$$

Explain why the rate of reaction decreases over the 5 days.
questions.answer:
As $H^+$ reacts, its concentration falls, and the readily accessible carbonate on the surface of the limestone is used up (reducing effective surface area). Both reduce the frequency of successful collisions between $H^+$ and carbonate, so the rate decreases until the mass is constant.

*Note: the school states the acid is the limiting reactant, but 200 mL of 0.1 M HNO₃ could dissolve about 1.0 g of CaCO₃, far more than the 0.17 g lost, so the acid cannot have been exhausted.*

questions.question:
A student investigated how acid affects limestone (mostly calcium carbonate, with small amounts of calcium sulfate). Pieces of limestone were placed in 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid in three beakers and 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid in three others, as shown. Each day the limestone was removed, washed, dried, weighed and replaced.

The student hypothesised that sulfuric acid would cause a larger mass loss than nitric acid. Justify this hypothesis.
questions.answer:
Sulfuric acid is diprotic while nitric acid is monoprotic, so equal volumes of equal concentration provide more $H^+$ from $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ (up to twice as much). More $H^+$ can react with more $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$:

$\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2H^+ \rightarrow Ca^{2+} + H_2O + CO_2}$

questions.question:
A student investigated how acid affects limestone (mostly calcium carbonate, with small amounts of calcium sulfate). Pieces of limestone were placed in 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid in three beakers and 200 mL of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid in three others, as shown. Each day the limestone was removed, washed, dried, weighed and replaced.

Unexpectedly, more mass was lost in nitric acid than in sulfuric acid. Using solubility rules and $K_{sp}$ data, suggest an explanation. Use equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
$\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) + 2HNO_3(aq) \rightarrow Ca(NO_3)_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)}$

$\mathrm{CaCO_3(s) + H_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow CaSO_4(s) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)}$

Calcium nitrate is soluble, but calcium sulfate is only sparingly soluble ($K_{sp}=4.93\times10^{-5}$). In sulfuric acid a layer of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ deposits on the limestone, blocking acid from reaching the carbonate and slowing or stopping the reaction. No such layer forms in nitric acid.

questions.question: Fuels can be obtained from a variety of sources. Assess the benefits and limitations of using ethanol as a fuel compared with ONE other fuel source.
questions.answer:
**Comparison: ethanol (from fermented crops) with petrol (octane, from crude oil).**

Benefits of ethanol:
- Renewable: made by fermenting glucose from crops such as sugar cane, whereas petrol comes from a finite resource.
- The crops absorb $CO_2$ by photosynthesis, offsetting part of the $CO_2$ released on combustion.
- It contains oxygen and needs less $O_2$ per mole, so it burns more completely, producing less CO and soot.

$\mathrm{C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O}$

$\mathrm{C_8H_{18} + \tfrac{25}{2}O_2 \rightarrow 8CO_2 + 9H_2O}$

Limitations of ethanol:
- Lower energy content (about 30 kJ g⁻¹ against 46–48 kJ g⁻¹ for octane), so more fuel and more frequent refuelling are needed.
- Crops compete with food for arable land and water.
- Farming, transport and distillation currently use fossil fuels, so it is not carbon neutral.
- Most engines need modification to run on high ethanol blends; infrastructure favours petrol.

**Assessment:** ethanol is a worthwhile partial replacement (e.g. E10 blends) that reduces fossil-fuel use, but land demand and low energy density mean it cannot fully replace petrol.

*Note: the school quotes 20.6 kJ g⁻¹ for ethanol; the value is about 29.6 kJ g⁻¹.*

questions.question:
Gold mining often uses cyanide ($CN^-$) to help remove gold from ore. A scientist tested whether water in a river near a gold mine contained excessive cyanide (maximum allowable level for drinking water: 0.5 mg/L).

**Test 1:** A 200.00 mL river sample was diluted to 1000.00 mL and titrated with 0.0100 M silver nitrate. Initially silver nitrate combines with $CN^-$ to form $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$ (a colourless complex). Once all the $CN^-$ is used up, silver nitrate reacts with $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$ to form AgCN, a white precipitate. The burette was filled to a reading of 60.00 mL and read 42.43 mL at the end. A blank titration required 0.870 mL of $AgNO_3$ for precipitation.

**Test 2:** The titration was repeated on a fresh, undiluted 200.00 mL sample, following the endpoint by potential and, separately, by UV absorbance (Figure 1).

**Test 3:** UV-Vis spectroscopy was used to measure the cyanide concentration after oxidation with chlorine (Figure 2). An undiluted sample was used in a 1.00 cm cuvette; the molar absorptivity was $5.87\times10^4\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$.

Examine the results and concentrations obtained in each experiment. Evaluate the scientist's methods and results.
questions.answer:
**Test 1**

$V(AgNO_3)=(60.00-42.43)-0.87=16.70$ mL, $n(Ag^+)=1.67\times10^{-4}$ mol

$\mathrm{Ag^+ + 2CN^- \rightarrow [Ag(CN)_2]^-}$, so $n(CN^-)=3.34\times10^{-4}$ mol (all from the original 200 mL)

$c=1.67\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ $=43.4$ mg/L

**Test 2**

Both curves give an endpoint of about 16.0 mL.

$n(CN^-)=2\times0.0103\times0.0160=3.30\times10^{-4}$ mol, $c=1.65\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ $=43$ mg/L

**Test 3**

Peak reading about 103: $c=\dfrac{A}{\varepsilon l}=\dfrac{103}{5.87\times10^4}=1.75\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ $\approx46$ mg/L

*Note: an absorbance of 103 is not physically possible (it would mean essentially no light is transmitted, and Beer's law is linear only up to about 1–2). The axis must be mislabelled; the calculation above is the intended one, as in the school's solution.*

All results (about 44 mg/L) are far above 0.5 mg/L.

**Evaluation**

- *Validity:* three independent principles measure the same quantity. The blank in Test 1 corrects for the reagent needed to produce a visible precipitate. Test 3 lacks a calibration curve and blank, and its reading is outside the valid range, so it is weakest.
- *Reliability:* no test was repeated, so reliability cannot be established within a method; agreement between methods is some support. Replicates and averaging are needed.
- *Accuracy:* instrumental endpoint detection (Test 2) removes subjective judgement of the first cloudiness in Test 1; reading from a small graph limits precision. Standards of known cyanide concentration would test accuracy, and more samples from several sites and times are needed to represent the river.

Overall the methods agree well enough to conclude confidently that cyanide greatly exceeds the safe limit, although the exact value is less certain.

questions.question: An equilibrium has the generalised equation $\mathrm{2AB_2 \rightleftharpoons A_2B_4}$, $\Delta H=-250$ kJ mol⁻¹. At time $t=3$ s the temperature was increased. Both Le Chatelier's principle and collision theory state that the position of equilibrium would change. Compare these TWO theories to explain the effect of the temperature change, including the effect of temperature on activation energy and reaction rate.
questions.answer:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** the system shifts to counteract the change. The forward reaction is exothermic, so on heating the equilibrium shifts left (the endothermic direction) to absorb some of the added heat, giving more $AB_2$. It predicts the direction of the shift but says nothing about rates or why it happens.

**Collision theory:** reaction needs collisions with correct orientation and energy at least equal to $E_a$. Raising temperature does not change $E_a$, but increases particle kinetic energy, so collisions are more frequent and a much larger fraction exceed $E_a$. Both forward and reverse rates increase. The reverse (endothermic) reaction has the larger $E_a$, so its fraction of successful collisions increases proportionally more. The reverse rate exceeds the forward rate until they become equal again at a position further left.

**Comparison:** both predict a shift towards $AB_2$; Le Chatelier is a quick qualitative rule, while collision theory explains the mechanism and the faster attainment of the new equilibrium.

questions.question: An equilibrium has the generalised equation $\mathrm{2AB_2 \rightleftharpoons A_2B_4}$, $\Delta H=-250$ kJ mol⁻¹. At time $t=3$ s the temperature was increased. The new equilibrium was reached at 6 s. The graph shows the concentrations up to $t=3$ s. Sketch the concentrations after $t=3$ s.
questions.answer: $[AB_2]$ rises smoothly and $[A_2B_4]$ falls smoothly from $t=3$ s, with no sudden jump (temperature change does not alter concentrations instantly). The change in $[AB_2]$ is twice that in $[A_2B_4]$ (e.g. 0.65 → 0.69 M and 0.59 → 0.57 M), and both are constant from 6 s.

questions.question: An equilibrium has the generalised equation $\mathrm{2AB_2 \rightleftharpoons A_2B_4}$, $\Delta H=-250$ kJ mol⁻¹. At time $t=3$ s the temperature was increased. What is the effect of the increase in temperature on the value of $K_{eq}$?
questions.answer: $K_{eq}$ decreases: the forward reaction is exothermic, so at higher temperature the equilibrium contains relatively less product.

questions.question: Describe an investigation to determine the $K_{eq}$ of a chemical equilibrium system. Include an equation and approximate results in your answer.
questions.answer:
**System:** $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + SCN^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons FeSCN^{2+}(aq)}$ (blood red)

**Method**
1. Make standards of known $[FeSCN^{2+}]$ (using a large excess of $Fe^{3+}$) and measure absorbance near 450 nm to draw a calibration curve.
2. Mix 5.0 mL of 0.0020 M $\mathrm{Fe(NO_3)_3}$ with 5.0 mL of 0.0020 M KSCN at constant temperature.
3. Measure absorbance and read $[FeSCN^{2+}]_{eq}$ from the curve.
4. Repeat several times and average.

**Approximate results:** initial $[Fe^{3+}]=[SCN^-]=1.0\times10^{-3}$ M; measured $[FeSCN^{2+}]_{eq}=1.1\times10^{-4}$ M, so $[Fe^{3+}]=[SCN^-]=8.9\times10^{-4}$ M.

$$K_{eq}=\frac{[FeSCN^{2+}]}{[Fe^{3+}][SCN^-]}=\frac{1.1\times10^{-4}}{(8.9\times10^{-4})^2}\approx1.4\times10^2$$

questions.question: 21 mL of 0.210 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid was added to 31 mL of 0.210 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide. What was the pH of the resulting solution?
The pH of a 0.125 mol L⁻¹ solution of benzoic acid ($\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$) is 2.83. Calculate the $K_a$ of benzoic acid.
questions.answer:
$\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5COO^- + H^+}$

$[H^+]=[C_6H_5COO^-]=10^{-2.83}=1.48\times10^{-3}$ M

$[C_6H_5COOH]=0.125-0.00148=0.1235$ M

$$K_a=\frac{(1.48\times10^{-3})^2}{0.1235}=1.77\times10^{-5}$$

(Neglecting the dissociation in the denominator gives $1.75\times10^{-5}$, also acceptable as it is under 5%.)

questions.question: The pH of a 0.125 mol L⁻¹ solution of benzoic acid ($\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$) is 2.83. Given $K_a=1.77\times10^{-5}$, calculate the p$K_a$ of benzoic acid.
The pH of a 0.125 mol L⁻¹ solution of benzoic acid ($\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$) is 2.83. Calculate the percentage dissociation of the benzoic acid.

A student found the model shown to help explain how an acetic acid/acetate ion buffer system works. Assess the effectiveness of the model in explaining the chemistry of buffers. Include an equation in your answer.
questions.answer:
$\mathrm{CH_3COOH(aq) + H_2O(l) \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^-(aq) + H_3O^+(aq)}$

**Strengths:** it shows a buffer containing comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base. Adding $H_3O^+$ converts $CH_3COO^-$ into $CH_3COOH$ (equilibrium shifts left); adding $OH^-$ converts $CH_3COOH$ into $CH_3COO^-$ (it removes $H_3O^+$, so the equilibrium shifts right). The changing bar heights show this and the conservation of total amount.

**Limitations:** it does not show $H_3O^+$ or the pH staying nearly constant, gives no equilibrium or dynamic nature, no explanation via Le Chatelier's principle, no equation, and does not show buffer capacity (large additions would exhaust one component).

**Assessment:** it is a useful simple visual of what changes, but only moderately effective, since it does not explain why the pH resists change.

questions.question:
Propene is an important starting material for many products. A student wrote these notes about propene and its products. Explain the student's notes. Include equations in your answer.

**Reactions:** $\mathrm{C_3H_6 \rightarrow C_3H_7Cl \rightarrow C_3H_8O \rightarrow C_3H_6O}$. Various reactants and conditions are needed.

**Molar enthalpy of combustion:** $\mathrm{C_3H_8O}$ undergoes complete and incomplete combustion. In the classroom, 180 mL of water was heated using 1.05 g of $\mathrm{C_3H_8O}$, raising the water temperature by 42 °C. In the SI data book at 25.0 °C, the standard molar entropy was 193 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the molar Gibbs free energy was −2078.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

**Boiling point:** $\mathrm{C_3H_8O}$ has a higher boiling point than $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$.
questions.answer:
**Reaction pathway**

1. Addition of HCl to propene (room temperature); the major product is 2-chloropropane (minor: 1-chloropropane):
$\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2 + HCl \rightarrow CH_3CHClCH_3}$
2. Substitution with dilute aqueous NaOH, heated under reflux, giving propan-2-ol:
$\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3 + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3CH(OH)CH_3 + NaCl}$
3. Oxidation of the secondary alcohol with acidified $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ under reflux, giving propanone:
$\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3 + [O] \rightarrow CH_3COCH_3 + H_2O}$

(Starting from 1-chloropropane would give propan-1-ol, then propanal or propanoic acid.)

**Combustion**

Complete: $\mathrm{C_3H_8O + \tfrac92O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O}$

Incomplete: $\mathrm{C_3H_8O + 3O_2 \rightarrow 3CO + 4H_2O}$ or $\mathrm{C_3H_8O + \tfrac32O_2 \rightarrow 3C + 4H_2O}$

Classroom: $q=mc\Delta T=180\times4.18\times42=31.6$ kJ; $n=1.05/60.09=0.01747$ mol; $\Delta H=-q/n\approx-1.8\times10^3$ kJ mol⁻¹

Data book (intended calculation): $\Delta H=\Delta G+T\Delta S=-2078.5+298.15\times0.193=-2.02\times10^3$ kJ mol⁻¹

*Note: 193 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is described as a standard molar entropy, which is not the entropy change of combustion; the question (and school solution) treats it as $\Delta S$.*

The classroom magnitude is lower because of heat lost to the surroundings and apparatus, incomplete combustion, and evaporation of fuel.

**Boiling point**

Propan-2-ol has an O–H group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other (plus dipole–dipole and dispersion forces). Propanone has a polar C=O but no H bonded to O, so only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act between its molecules. More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces in propan-2-ol, so it has the higher boiling point.
